Legalism. A Chinese political philosophy emphasizing strict laws, centralized state power, and absolute obedience to rulers, developed during the Warring States period from four hundred seventy-five to two hundred twenty-one BCE. Legalist thinkers rejected moral appeals and Confucian virtue as insufficient for governing. Instead, they advocated for harsh punishments, meritocratic bureaucracy, and total state control over all aspects of society.

Legalism emerged in response to the chaos of the Warring States period, proposing that only through strict law and centralized authority could order be achieved amid perpetual conflict. Key Legalist thinkers included Han Feizi, Shang Yang, and Li Si, who crafted theories of absolute state power and reward-punishment mechanisms to control human behavior. They rejected Confucian emphasis on moral cultivation, ritual propriety, and benevolent governance as naive and impractical, insisting instead that only fear of punishment motivated obedience.

Legalists advocated a system of rewards and punishments so severe and predictable that subjects would be motivated purely by self-interest to obey all state laws without exception. Shihuangdi of the Qin Dynasty implemented Legalism wholesale, creating the world's first centralized, bureaucratized empire with standardized weights, measures, writing, and roads. The Qin's brutal application included book burning, mass conscription, harsh punishments, and Legalist scholars buried alive, serving as an extreme model of authoritarian governance.

Though the Qin Dynasty's collapse raised questions about Legalism's viability, subsequent dynasties adapted its centralized bureaucratic framework while moderating its harshness through Confucian influence. Legalism shaped the Qin Dynasty that fully embraced it, influenced the Han Dynasty which moderated extreme Legalism with Confucian ideas, and was guided by Shihuangdi the Qin emperor who employed Legalist advisor Li Si to consolidate imperial power.
